53a3963a8550.title: ArchiMate models — every view, element and relationship a node
53a3963a8550.content: Skill archimate-models: ArchiMate models as knowledge-graph content: how a layer declares the Archi models it holds, what the archimate subgraph gives every model, view, element and relationship (an IRI, a thin page, and every view drawn as SVG from the model’s own diagram, and its metamodel derived and checked), how to version the models, how to wire them into a folio’s staging build and navbar, how to count and lower the crossed lines in a view before committing it, why every view carries a plain-language key, why names are the source’s own terms linked to their SKOS concepts, and why no Java, no Archi CLI and no Archi HTML report is ever part of the pipeline. Read before adding, authoring, publishing or rendering an .archimate file, before citing an ArchiMate element from prose, and before reaching for Archi’s own tooling in CI. Named by: Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5), Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5) . Skill id: archimate-models · Package: ui-core · Subgraph: cat-harness/archimate/ · Tools: archimate-check, archimate-metamodel, archimate-blocks, archimate-pages, archimate-crossings, archimate-detangle, archimate-actors · Process: archimate-publish (processes/ui/archimate-publish.bpmn) .

809788c9ed05.title: The rule
809788c9ed05.content: An ArchiMate model is content, and every view, element and relationship in it is a node. The model is authored in Archi and committed where it is held. Everything a reader sees is made from it on each build, by the archimate subgraph, in TypeScript, with no tool installed: . | node | IRI (under the graph’s path) | page |   | . | model | <m>.jsonld | <m>/ | views; elements by layer | . | view | <m>/views/<id>.jsonld | <m>/views/<slug>/ | the drawing, <m>/views/<id>.svg | . | element | <m>/elements/<id>.jsonld | <m>/elements/<slug>/ | documentation, properties, relationships, views it is in | . | relationship | <m>/relationships/<id>.jsonld | <m>/relationships/<id>/ | its ends, the views it is drawn in | . Ids are Archi’s own (id-<32 hex>). An element therefore keeps its IRI across a model’s versions wherever Archi kept its id — the property the RA mapper’s mappings already depend on. Never rewrite one; the reader refuses an id that is not filename-safe rather than minting one nobody chose.

85f52142d795.title: Readable page paths: slugs, worked out each build
85f52142d795.content: The IRI stays the id; only the page is at a slug. A view’s or element’s page is at <m>/views/1-central-health-workforce-registry/, while its node keeps <m>/views/<id>.jsonld. Cite the IRI when a link must last: the page path is for reading. Relationships keep id paths, since almost none are named. Slugs are worked out from the names on every build (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/slugs.ts). Nothing is committed and nothing redirects, so: . | a rename moves the page, and the old path is gone (a clean break; there are no <m>/views/<id>/ page paths); | on a clash the object first in the model keeps the plain slug and a later one gets -<first hex of its id>; | an author can choose a slug in Archi with a slug property (lower-case words joined by -); a malformed one, or two objects choosing the same one, is refused rather than rewritten; | an object with no readable name keeps its id as its path. | . Do not put slugs in the IRIs: the mapper keys on the ids, and a rename would move an IRI.

ee56fb9f0ce8.title: The metamodel is derived, never drawn
ee56fb9f0ce8.content: Do not draw a metamodel view. Which element types a model uses, and which relationships it draws between them, is computed from the model by the Tool archimate-metamodel (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/metamodel.ts): . | every element type, with how many elements it has; | every pattern (source type, relationship, target type), with its count and the ids of the relationships that follow it; | for each pattern, whether ArchiMate allows it, from Appendix B of ArchiMate 3.2 as Archi holds it (archimate/schemas/archimate-relationships.json, MIT, written only by scripts/import-archi-relationships.ts; to adopt a newer table, re-run it on a newer Archi checkout); | the placeholder elements: an element named after its own type (“Goal”, “Application Component (MS)”). They are how a metamodel gets drawn by hand inside a model, so they and their relationships are listed and kept out of the patterns. A Grouping or Junction left with its default name is not one. | . archimate-pages draws the same result on each model’s Metamodel in use page (<m>/metamodel/), linked from the model page and the rail: a class diagram laid out from DOT by Graphviz in WebAssembly (@hpcc-js/wasm-graphviz, no binary, no JVM), with the same diagram as DOT, Mermaid and JSON beside it (<m>/metamodel.dot|.mmd|.json|.svg), and tables of the types and patterns, each pattern linking its relationships. archimate-metamodel --check fails when a relationship follows a pattern ArchiMate does not allow. Placeholders are reported, never fatal: a model is its authors’, so removing a hand-drawn metamodel view is their call. Cite the derived page instead of the view in the meantime. The steps run in this order, all in the pipeline lane of process archimate-publish: archimate-check, then archimate-metamodel --check, then archimate-pages. A refused relationship goes back to the model’s author.

c8015a7e2fa4.title: Actors come first; the model points at them
c8015a7e2fa4.content: The SMART Guidelines order is fixed: a DAK’s L2 generic personas become the IG’s L3 FHIR ActorDefinitions, and the architecture realizes them (DPI-H RA §4.3.2). So the ActorDefinitions are written in the IG, from the DAK personas, and the model only points at them. A model author tags the box that realizes an actor in Archi with the property fhir-actor, whose value is the actor’s canonical URL (fhir-actor = http://smart.who.int/ra/ActorDefinition/FacilityRegistry), the same way an element carries skosConcept. | Never generate an ActorDefinition, or any FSH, from the model. When the model has a box with no actor, the actor is missing from the IG: add it there, from the persona, then tag the box. | Never decide which box realizes which actor from names. That is the model authors’ call, made in Archi. A box may realize several actors (one tag each), and an actor may be realized by several boxes. | A #system actor goes on an application or technology element (an ApplicationComponent, an ApplicationInterface, a Node). A #person actor goes on a BusinessActor or BusinessRole. Any other kind of element cannot realize an actor. | Check the tags with the Tool archimate-actors: bun run cat archimate:actors --instance . --model <id>. It fails on a value that is not a canonical URL, a tag that names no ActorDefinition of the IG, an element kind that cannot be an actor, and a type mismatch. It warns about each ActorDefinition that no element realizes. With --strict that warning becomes a failure. --json gives element → actors and actor → elements, for the pages’ back-links. | . Data objects follow the same rule. A data object points at an existing logical model with logical-model = <canonical>. Write the logical model in the IG first. Never derive a logical model from the model’s boxes. The data object’s class diagram will be generated from that logical model once the IG holds one, so tag the data object now and do not draw the diagram.

074284d1df4d.title: A document’s tables and figures are drawn, not typed
074284d1df4d.content: A table or figure in the document that restates the model is generated from data by the Tool archimate-blocks, and --check keeps it from drifting. | Relationship rules and types live once, as an archimate-relationship-rules/v1 file in the archimate directory (cat-harness-tools/archimate/schemas/rules.ts). The document’s rules table and relationship-types table are drawn from it (config tables), with the caption and footnotes left as the editors wrote them. | The rules are in charge, not the model. For a rules table that names a model, the Tool reports rules the model never uses, relationships no rule covers, rules ArchiMate’s own table refuses, and relationship types the rules use but the document never explains. The editors decide, link by link, whether to fix the model or add a rule; nothing is rewritten from the model. | A figure that is a view names an svg in its figures entry. The Tool writes the view there with the same renderer as the view’s page, and the block shows that SVG instead of a picture. Check the drawing against the published figure first: element names in the model must match the document’s. | .

ffacbe6c99a6.title: Untangle every view you touch
ffacbe6c99a6.content: A change to a view never adds tangles, and every view you touch leaves with no more than it came with. A tangle is a line crossing another line, or a line running through a box that is not one of its ends and does not hold one. Groups (bands) are not boxes here; a line may cross a band. Every time you add, move or re-route anything in a view: . | Count before. bun run cat archimate:crossings --model <file> --view <id or page slug> lists each tangle by the boxes it joins. | Make the change. | Let the tool lower it. bun run cat archimate:detangle --model <file> --view <id or page slug> reports what it would do: re-route lines (straight, an L, or a Z through a free lane between rows) and swap same-size boxes in the same row or column. It keeps a change only if the count goes down. Add --apply to write it, or --routes-only when the boxes’ places carry meaning (an order, a flow). | Look at the drawing (gen-archimate-pages.ts --out, or the view’s SVG) before and after. The count is a gate, not taste: undo a swap that breaks a reading order, and fix by hand what the tool cannot (it never adds, resizes or regroups boxes). | Count after, and say both numbers in the PR: “view X: 10 crossings, 13 through a box → 1, 2”. More tangles after than before is a finding to fix before review, not a note. | . Ways to untangle by hand, in the order to try them: . | Put a box beside the boxes it is joined to: a line’s ends in neighbouring rows, not across the view. | Order a row like the row it connects to (the order of the boxes above), so lines between the two rows run parallel. | Route a long line along the gap between rows or bands, with right-angle bendpoints, rather than diagonally across boxes. | Nest instead of drawing a line where the notation allows it (composition, aggregation, assignment, realization): a box drawn inside another already says how they relate, and the renderer draws no line for it. | When nothing else works, a view shows too much: split it. | .

f7b626a6a926.title: Every view carries a key for readers who do not know ArchiMate
f7b626a6a926.content: Readers of a view are mostly not architects. Every rendered view carries a plain-language key below it, saying what each colour, shape, line and end used ON THAT VIEW means, in words a reader without ArchiMate understands (“Realization: makes real, or achieves”), not the specification’s terms alone. render-view.ts draws it by default, keyed only to what the view uses. Do not turn it off for a published view, and do not export a view without it. When the renderer gains a new mark, the key gains its line in the same change.

dd3a89e2235f.title: Names are the source’s own terms, linked to their concept
dd3a89e2235f.content: An element or view named from a source uses the source’s own term, and links to that term’s SKOS concept. Not our paraphrase, shortening or merger of two terms. When a model depicts a module of a handbook, the box is named as the handbook names it, and the element carries the concept’s IRI (a property, e.g. concept = the skos:Concept IRI in the source’s glossary scheme) so its page links to the definition. | No concept for the term yet: add it to the source’s glossary scheme first, from the source’s own words, then name the element. | The source’s term is too long for a box: keep the full term as the name and let the renderer wrap it; a short form goes in skos:altLabel, never in place of the name. | Our term and the source’s disagree: that is a content decision (term-disagreement), not something to settle by renaming in Archi. | .

77d172257e28.title: The model is never a source of the glossary
77d172257e28.content: An authored model depicts concepts; it never defines them. Meaning lives in the SKOS glossary, read from the source documents. So: . | Never write a term, label, definition, focus or relationship into a glossary from a model someone authored in Archi. An element with no term is a term to add from the source’s own words, not from the box. | The glossary may drive the model (archimate-from-glossary, a content layer’s Tool): names, documentation and relationships flow from the terms into the model, and Archi keeps the layout. | The term pages’ “depicted by” links read skosConcept on each build and write nothing into the glossary, so they are allowed. | The one exception is an ingested model, received from elsewhere and held as a source under the layer’s library/. It may seed the glossary once (archimate-from-glossary --seed --from library/…), like any other ingested source. The Tool refuses --seed on any model outside library/. | .

41540dffa9ee.title: No Java, no Archi CLI, no Archi report — ever
41540dffa9ee.content: The Archi command line (com.archimatetool.commandline.app) renders an HTML report and view images, and it is not part of any pipeline here: . | it needs a JVM, a virtual display (xvfb) and a ~200 MB download on every run — too heavy for CI, and impossible in a web client, which is where an agent or a reader working in the browser is; | its views are raster images nobody can link into, and its pages are not nodes: nothing it writes has an IRI in the graph. | . render-view.ts draws the same views from the same coordinates — the bounds Archi stores for every box (made absolute, since Archi nests a child’s bounds in its parent’s) and the relative bendpoints it stores for every line — into SVG in ArchiMate’s notation, every box a link to its element. The reader handles Archi’s native XML and its zipped archive with node:zlib. If a view ever needs something the renderer does not draw, extend the renderer; do not bring Archi back into a workflow. The same reasoning applies to any other Java-only ArchiMate tooling (jArchi scripts, coArchi). Authors use Archi on their own machines; the pipeline never does.

9f8dec037de4.title: Versions — one folder per SemVer version
9f8dec037de4.content: A model is named for the version of the thing it describes. In a WHO IG repository that is the version: in sushi-config.yaml: archimate/0.2.0/, with earlier drafts as SemVer pre-releases (0.2.0-draft.1, …). The model id in the config is that version, so …/archimate/0.2.0/elements/<id>.jsonld is both versioned and stable. Never name a folder v2, prev1 or current: a label that says nothing about what it is a version of invites two identical models under two names.

d2c340a4931d.title: In a folio’s build
d2c340a4931d.content: bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/archimate/scripts/check-archimate.ts --instance . bun run <platform>/cat-harness-tools/archimate/scripts/gen-archimate-pages.ts --instance . --out _site . Run both in the staging build, after the document site is built and before the navbar pass, so the pages are railed like every other page. --out is the normal mode: a few models yield thousands of pages, which belong in a build, not a commit. gen-archimate-pages.ts without --out writes into the graph and --check gates it, as the openapi subgraph does, for a layer small enough to commit its pages.

3369eda8e3d1.title: Citing the model from prose
3369eda8e3d1.content: Link the element’s or the view’s page, never a copy of a picture. A view’s SVG links relative to its own address, so it can also be embedded in a document as a figure (<m>/views/<id>.svg) and stay current with the model. Where the document and the model disagree — a figure in the text that is not a view in the model — that is a finding for the model’s authors, not something to paper over with an exported image.

eb528d441858.title: What is not read yet
eb528d441858.content: The Open Group exchange format; custom images and fonts on a diagram (each box names its type in its corner instead of Archi’s icons — the icons are the tool’s artwork, not the notation’s); sketch and canvas views; ingesting a model from another repository. Each is an extension of schemas/archimate.ts or render-view.ts, in TypeScript.

468b313c0165.title: Do not
468b313c0165.content: . | Draw a metamodel, or any class diagram of the model’s types, by hand: cite the derived “Metamodel in use” page. | Run Archi, a JVM or xvfb in a workflow to render a model. | Commit exported view images beside a model; they go stale on the next edit. | Name model folders by anything but the version they describe. | Declare the archimate typology in a layer whose platform pin predates it. | Commit a change to a view without counting its tangles before and after. | Publish a view without its key, or name an element from a source in words the source does not use. | .

751dd0517aa4.content: . | Execute test plans and test scripts | Run the content type’s own build, extraction, and verification checks (as specified by the layer that ships the content type) | Dispatch the repo’s CI workflow on your branch and fold the result into the PR — see below; a local build is not CI green | Test cross-component integration | Run regression tests against previous versions | Document test results | .

ff2f45b986cb.title: Running CI, not just assuming it
ff2f45b986cb.content: A local build runs on a warm cache, your toolchain and your flags; CI runs cold on its own. A local green is evidence about your machine, not about the branch. Push, then dispatch the workflow against your branch (gh workflow run <workflow>.yml --ref <branch>, or the actions_run_trigger MCP tool), wait for it, and record run URL + conclusion in the PR body. Red → fix and re-dispatch. If dispatch is refused for lack of actions: write, say so in the PR and give the command a maintainer should run. Also check when CI last ran (actions_list → list_workflow_runs): a workflow nothing dispatches can sit red on main while the content it checks stops building.

9578eace9d27.title: A green build only covers what the target reaches
9578eace9d27.content: Before reading “build green” as a claim about the corpus, check what the build target actually compiles. Build systems often default to narrow roots: the target compiles its root plus whatever that root imports, not every source in the directory. Where sources are found and what is built are separate settings. The check is cheap in any build system — count build artifacts against sources. A ratio far from 1 means the green is scoped, and any corpus-wide number read off that build — open-obligation counts, coverage, warning totals — is an undercount by construction. Say what the build covered, not just that it passed.

cc3dfba541b3.title: Where the results go — not into a commit
cc3dfba541b3.content: A test run’s results are derived: re-running the plan over the same tree and data reproduces them. They are kept where every derived QA result is kept — the orphan qa-reports branch, keyed by the commit they were computed on (main/<sha>/, pr/<n>/<sha>/), written by bun run cat qa:publish (the CI job qa-publish) and read back with bun run qa:fetch. Do not regenerate a results file in order to commit it. Two things a test run produces are not derived, and they stay on main: . | A reviewer’s judgement of a case — an SME or QC reviewer’s verdict, an agent’s adjudication — goes to test/attestations/ (qa-attestations/v1), because no re-run can reproduce it. | A certification — an accountable decision taken on a plan’s rollup — also stays on main, beside the attestations, and is then signed through qa-report-signing (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc). | . “Regression comparison” against a previous version is a comparison against its stored results: --against <ref> on a gate, or qa:fetch --ref for a report. A previous version with no stored entry is UNKNOWN — say so; never read it as “no regressions”.

665c5231d1eb.title: l2-dependency-choice
665c5231d1eb.content: Skill l2-dependency-choice: Stage 3 of smart-guideline-end-to-end: choose which existing DAKs (WHO’s, or a jurisdiction’s adaptation) the guideline builds on. From the L1 knowledge graph and any known candidates, one decision row per candidate DAK — reuse, adapt, extend or reject, with evidence and a reason — laid out as a decision-comparison table and put to the adjudicators as a DecisionRequest. Also defines the dependency decision row that stage 5 (l3-dependency-choice) uses at L3. Read before choosing, or recording, a DAK dependency. Named by: Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5), Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5) . Skill id: l2-dependency-choice · Package: authoring-who-smart-guidelines · Stage 3 of smart-guideline-end-to-end, task Task_DepsL2 of smart-guideline-end-to-end.bpmn (opt-in smart-base.collab). Adjudicated by the programme manager and the business analyst.

2e8ea147ad45.content: The contract is input.schema.json and output.schema.json. | In: stage 2’s l1Kg (recommendation-extraction’s output), and the candidate DAKs already known (candidates: packageId, version, uri, publisher). | Out: l2Dependencies: one dependencyRow per candidate, rejected ones included, the gaps, the comparison table and the decisionRequest. 709620816ee6.title: Adopting a methodology, and choosing between them
709620816ee6.content: Skill methodology-adoption: How a named external methodology enters the knowledge graph, and how an agent picks which one applies. Read before following a judgement method, before adopting a new one, and before writing a house method instead of adopting one. Named by: Conduct training, testing and roll-out (Ch 5, 5.1-5.4), Conduct training, testing and roll-out (Ch 5, 5.1-5.4) . A methodology is somebody else’s work, adopted whole. It is not a house process with a citation bolted on. The graph carries them as a distinct kind so that adopting one, replacing one and removing one are all ordinary operations. Methodologies are parallel ways of achieving the same process, chosen by context; each is formalised on its own and kept independent, so that other skills can incorporate it as a sub-graph.

872943660150.title: Parallel, not composable
872943660150.content: Two or more methodologies may answer the same question. Do not blend them. A composite — this one’s vocabulary, that one’s record, a third one’s filter — is a house method that cites nobody, and it inherits none of their authority while claiming all of it. So: pick one per decision, name it, and follow it.

31ca984bf1f6.title: Choosing which applies
31ca984bf1f6.content: First: is this a judgement, or a process? . Ask before the ladder. The ladder below is about how to decide something; a request for a change is not yet a decision but work needing agreed requirements before anything is built. Sent down the ladder, it lands on the catch-all rung and produces an options analysis for a question nobody has framed yet. Is somebody asking for a change, such that requirements have to be agreed before it is built? . If yes, the question is who is asking, and does the answer depend on what a folio says? . | A change to the platform’s own capability — a tool, a schema, a pipeline, a skill, a gate — raised by somebody building the tooling, whose answer does not depend on any folio’s subject matter → the software-development process methodology. | Requirements that come from stakeholders who must sign them off, tied to a folio’s domain → the stakeholder requirements methodology. | . Both answer request → agreed requirements, so they are parallel and must not be blended — the refusal below applies to this pair first and hardest. Which is which is stated in each one’s applies-when, not here, for the reason in §”Why this skill does not name them”. If no — the change is agreed and the question is how to decide something within it — continue to the ladder. Then the ladder . Ask in this order. The first yes decides. | Do the criteria recur, with the same inputs having to produce the same answer? → the computable methodology. A one-off tabled as if it recurs asserts a repeatability it does not have. | Is the question the certainty of a body of evidence behind a recommendation? → the evidence-grading methodology. Note this is about evidence, not about a design choice that happens to be uncertain. | Is the context a work item recording a decision? → the decision-record methodology. It constrains the record, not the method, so it composes with (1) or (4) rather than competing. | Otherwise — a one-off choice among candidate options → the decision-analysis methodology. | . If none fits, that is a finding, not a licence. Say which question the decision is and that no adopted methodology covers it. Do not improvise one and do not stretch the nearest fit: either is how a house method gets in. Why this skill does not name them . Naming each methodology here would couple this skill to the set, and the set is meant to be extractable: a methodology can be lifted out, or replaced, without a prose edit here. So the declared set is the contents of the methodology graph, read from the layer’s declaration. Ask for it; do not remember it.

a3c0c9b916df.title: Node, skill, or both?
a3c0c9b916df.content: An adopted methodology can produce up to two artefacts: . | you are writing | it is a node in the methodology graph | it is a skill | . | what the method IS — its vocabulary, its constraints, what it refuses | ✅ | ❌ | . | how to PERFORM it here — the extension element, the gate, the procedure | ❌ | ✅ | . | a house process with no external origin | ❌ | ✅ — and do not dress it as an adoption | . Most adoptions produce both, and the split is the same every time: the node is the method, the skill is this platform’s application of it. The skill names the node and does not restate it, because two files carrying one definition is two copies free to drift. Three worked cases: . | raci — both. The four letters and the one-Accountable rule are the method (node); reading R from the BPMN lane, the cat-harness.processes:raci element and check:raci are this platform’s application (skill). | crdm — both (methodologies/crdm.md). PHII’s three concentration areas (Business Process Analysis, Business Process Redesign, Requirements Definition), the Business Process Matrix, swimlane Task Flow Diagrams, and PATH’s activity-linked requirement structure are the external method (node, backed by library/phii-2023-crdm, library/phii-2021-defining-and-validating-requirements-guide, and library/path-2012-common-requirements-mhis-crdm); agentic facilitation, 7-dimension code impact analysis, work-item decomposition, and pull-request merge sign-off are this platform’s adaptation (crdm-requirements-workflow and crdm-requirements-template). | swot — both. | . A methodology in use with no node is invisible to the graph: check:methodology-evidence and every other reader of the methodology graph count nodes, not skills.

6d1990736f43.title: Adopting a new one — the ingestion process
6d1990736f43.content: . | Establish it is external and named. A methodology has an origin: authors, a publication, a standards body. If it has none, it is a house process — write it as a skill and do not dress it as an adoption. | Render it faithfully, and say where the rendering stops. The file carries what the method says, not a summary of what we liked. Where this platform adopts part of a method and refuses part, both halves are stated with the reason — a silent omission misrepresents the standard. | Declare its applicability. applies-when in the front matter, phrased so the selection question above can reach it, and saying what it is not for. | Place it by ownership, not by convenience. A domain-neutral method belongs to the harness; a domain method belongs to the repo that owns the domain. The separation plan decides, and the placement must make extraction literal — the directory lifts out, its declaration entry goes with it, and nothing else moves. | Declare the directory. A methodology outside a declared directory is invisible to every tool that reads the graph. | State its refusals. The part of a method a platform must not do is as load-bearing as the part it follows, and it is the part a later agent will breach first. | Ingest the source and cite it as evidence. origin names the work; evidence: library/<bib-slug> points at a copy a reader can open from this checkout. Use literature-search to find it and library-ingestion to bring it in. Where the source cannot be fetched, that is an outcome to report — a located-but-unreachable document, never a missing one — and the node keeps its origin with no evidence until somebody closes the gap. | .

9d9c027bdc9b.title: Extract the PROCESS, not the paper’s tools
9d9c027bdc9b.content: A source that presents a method through an implementation is presenting two things, and only one of them is the methodology. Render the method first, then decide which tools — existing or to be added — this platform should use to perform it. A node that adopted the source’s tool stack would be adopting an implementation and calling it a method, and it could never be falsified: the tools would work and the method would never be examined. hybrid-llm-deterministic is the worked case. Its source demonstrates the method in one tool with one model and one expression language; the node renders the rule/result inversion, the five safeguards and the bounded-truncation technique, and §”Where this rendering stops” names every tool it declined to adopt and why. The method survives replacing all of them, which is the test of whether you extracted a method at all. Ask it as: what would still be true if they had built it differently? What survives is the methodology. What does not is their engineering, and it belongs in the skill if anywhere — where this platform’s own tool choices already live. And say what the source does NOT establish. A demonstration is not an evaluation. Where a paper shows an approach working once, with no baseline and no measurement, the node records that no performance claim rests on it. Doing otherwise manufactures a finding the authors did not make — the same failure as §”Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured”, arriving through a citation instead.

bbd041ce9105.title: An origin nobody can open is not evidence
bbd041ce9105.content: A methodology’s justification is being somebody else’s named, external work, so its origin must resolve to a source a reader can open. bun run cat check:methodology-evidence is the axis that makes this visible, and test/results/methodology-evidence.qa-results.json is where it is recorded. It reports and does not gate on a missing source: whether a methodology whose source nobody can open may still be used is the owner’s call, and a gate failing on the whole corpus at once would be switched off. It does fail on front matter that does not validate, and on an evidence pointing at a bib-slug no library holds, because a citation that claims to resolve and does not is worse than none. The evidence is an input to SELECTION, not only to adoption. options-analysis.bpmn’s A_CheckEvidence reads it before the chosen methodology is applied. Adoption happens once; selection happens at every decision, and a source can stop being reachable in between. A contested origin is recorded as contested. methodologies/swot.md is the worked example: the usual attribution is repeated everywhere and its own source says no academic reference supports it, so the node declines to name an inventor: flattening that into a fact would carry the authority of a citation while resting on nothing.

5abc1518de02.title: Refusals
5abc1518de02.content: . | Never blend two methodologies into one procedure. Parallel means parallel. | Never adopt a methodology by naming it. A citation with no rendered method is an appeal to authority that no reader can check. | Never quantify a judgement to make it look measured. Where a method scores and sums, this platform adopts the structure and refuses the arithmetic: a total reads as a measurement, and the weights were invented. This is the same rule as never quoting a count from prose as though it were evidence. | Never let a rejected option go unrecorded. Whichever methodology was used, the alternatives and why they lost are part of the output — the same argument bean-coordination makes for scrapped over deleted. | Never write a method from recall and cite a paper nobody fetched. Read the source, or say you read it through another and mark each attribution second-hand. See literature-search §”Never fill the gap with recall”. | .

2c4c951cdd7b.title: Running a test plan — from a request to a signed certification
2c4c951cdd7b.content: Skill test-plan-execution: Run a test-plan/v1 against a system under test and take it to a certification decision — the five lanes of test-plan-execution.bpmn (requester, tester, untainted checker, certifier, attestation service), how the test data is bound, what the run and the report must record, the facts the certification table reads, and the kg-audit criteria that judge a run afterwards. Read before executing a plan, re-executing a sample, or certifying a result. Named by: Conduct training, testing and roll-out (Ch 5, 5.1-5.4), Conduct training, testing and roll-out (Ch 5, 5.1-5.4) . Skill id: test-plan-execution · Package: sdlc-core · Process: test-plan-execution.bpmn · Decision: test-certification.dmn . A system is tested against a plan, by somebody who is not the system, and certified by somebody who did not run the test. Everything below is that sentence made operational. This skill is the PROCESS. How to write a test is test-engineer; how a folio’s content is tested is content-test; why the checker sees only a controlled context is untainted-verification; how a signature is routed by reach is qa-report-signing. Read those for their halves — this one does not restate them.

efe16247c66c.title: The nodes, and who points at whom
efe16247c66c.content: | node | schema | where it lives | . | the plan | test-plan/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-plan.ts | authored content (test-plan kind) | . | the system under test | the systemUnderTest facet on an actor — schemas/kg/skill-package.ts | scenarios/actors/*.json | . | the run | folio-test-run/v1 with plan + sut — schemas/sdlc/test-run.ts | the declared qa directory | . | the report | test-report/v1 — schemas/sdlc/test-report.ts | the qa-reports branch, tests/<plan>/<sut>/<run>/ | . | the certification | a judgement, qa-attestations/v1 | the declared attestations graph, on main | . The run points at the plan; the plan names no run. A plan is reused across runs and systems, so a back-pointer would turn authored content into live state. Same direction for the report → run and the certification → report. The platform model is FHIR-free. FHIR R5 TestPlan informed test-plan/v1 and is a DOWNSTREAM export target, in the FHIR IG layer. Never read a FHIR TestPlan as the source of a plan here.

5fbd27af746b.title: The system under test is a facet, not a role
5fbd27af746b.content: Being tested is not a lane anybody takes on. An actor that can be executed — agent or system, never a person or an external — declares: . // an illustration, not a declared actor { "id": "example-mcp-tool", "kind": "system", "reach": "internet", "systemUnderTest": { "kind": "tool", "version": "0.1.0" } } . kind is the closed list SUT_KINDS (skill, agent, tool, machine, ig, process) — the same vocabulary as a plan’s scope.kind, so the two are compared, not translated. Reach is the actor’s own reach, read by sutRefFor; absent is unknown, never internet.

d3e819b0c926.title: The five lanes
d3e819b0c926.content: | lane | role | does | . | Requester / SUT | test-requester | asks for certification of system S against plan P, naming P’s id and version | . | Tester | tester | resolves P, binds its data, executes every case, writes the run and the report | . | Untainted checker | untainted-checker | re-executes a SAMPLE of cases, blind to the tester’s verdicts | . | Certifier | certifier | applies the plan’s exitCriteria table, then records the decision | . | Attestation service | attestation-service | signs, via qa-report-signing.bpmn, and files the certification | . The tester is untainted from the system under test. The SUT may request; it may never be the tester, the checker or the certifier, and it never writes a verdict about itself — test-report/v1 refuses a reviewer whose id or actor is the SUT’s actor, and test-sut-not-self-judged audits it. Tester . | Resolve the plan. P parses as test-plan/v1.1 (a test-plan/v1 plan still parses, deprecated), names at least one req: requirement, its exitCriteria.decision resolves to a decision in a .dmn that exists, and its scope.kind matches the SUT actor’s facet kind. A plan that does not resolve is not run. Every case names the .feature it is written in, and every test that executes it carries that file’s @test: tag (test-engineer). | Bind the test data (test-data-sets). A fixed set is a committed path and is evidence only once reviewed (isEvidence). A generated set is a template + params + seed and is never materialised into the repository. Both feed the run’s data hash; runner, configuration and scenario bank feed its process hash, and the two bases must be disjoint (buildTestRun refuses otherwise). | Execute. Every case is executed, or recorded skipped with a reason. A case with no verdict at the end of a terminal run is a finding, not an omission (checkAgainstPlan). | Write the run and the report. The run records plan {id, version} and sut {actor, version, reach}; the report rolls up per plan, never across plans, and testReportPath says where it goes. | . Untainted checker . Re-executes a sample of the cases from the plan and the data alone — never the tester’s verdicts — and reports agree, disagree or unknown. It RULES ON NOTHING (untainted-verification rule 3): the comparison is a fact the certification table reads, not a verdict the checker writes. Certifier . The gateway is computed. Pass the facts; never assert the branch — the engine refuses a hand-supplied outcome on a DMN gateway. | fact | from | . | reportStatus | the report’s status | . | dataHashKnown | the run’s data.hash is not unknown | . | unexecutedCases | checkAgainstPlan(...).filter(kind === "unexecuted-case").length | . | checker | the untainted checker’s agree / disagree / unknown | . | failedCases | rollup.fail | . | passedCases | rollup.pass | . The table returns certified, refused or undetermined. undetermined is the third state — a running or aborted report, an unknown data hash, an unexecuted case, a checker that disagreed or could not run, or a report in which nothing passed. It is never rendered as certified, and it is not a refusal either: it says the evidence does not decide, so nothing is signed. The certification decision is a judgement. The table says whether the exit criteria are met; the certifier — a person, a specialisation of stakeholder — records the decision, and it lives with the other judgements under the declared attestations graph, never on the qa-reports branch with derived results. Attestation service . Call_Sign runs qa-report-signing.bpmn unchanged; its route (API or a human release authority) is chosen there by the signer’s reach. Then the signed certification is filed under attestations.

7a14c1f38bf0.title: Wireframe design review
7a14c1f38bf0.content: Skill wireframe-design-review: Design a user interface (a page, a visualiser, a navbar) by the WireGen methodology: a written design intent, at least two mid-fidelity HTML candidates, each with a web AND a mobile layout, mechanical checks at both viewports, a blind per-criterion review, adjudication where reviewers disagree, and a recorded choice. Also how an EXISTING visualiser is wireframed as-is, so that every declared visualiser has a wireframe with a QA sidecar. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn. Called for Design use from CRDM (Process_CRDM_Requirements, Call_Wireframe) whenever a requirement changes a rendered surface, before anything is built. Named by: Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5), Undertake design and adaptation (Ch 4, 4.1-4.5) . Method: wiregen. Process: processes/ui/wireframe-design-review.bpmn.

f5e4fd68abb0.title: Where wireframes live
f5e4fd68abb0.content: | use | directory | . | As-is | <instance>/docs/wireframes/<topic>/, in the layer that declares the visualiser: cat-harness/docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for this harness’s own pages, and a content layer’s own docs/wireframes/<topic>/ for a page it declares | . | Design, from a CRDM request | docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/, beside the request’s proposal docs/proposals/<slug>.md: the candidates are assets of the proposal. When the proposal is filed (git mv to docs/requirements/, crdm-requirements-workflow (opt-in cat-harness.sdlc)), its asset directory moves with it in the same commit. | . Either directory holds: . | intent.md | one HTML file per candidate | authors.json, which reviewers are not shown | checks/: screenshots and the checker’s report | reviews/: one file per reviewer | . Each layer’s docs/wireframes/index.json maps the visualiser refs that layer declares to the wireframe that covers each. bun run cat check:wireframes reads every such index in the checkout, writes the QA sidecar (test/results/wireframes.qa-results.json) and fails on any gap. A wireframe sits with its page because an index naming another layer’s page reads as an undeclared ref wherever that layer is not mounted; another layer’s wireframes are reported as <instance>/<topic>.

b3d1b51d2d7b.content: | use | candidates | review | . | Design: a new or changed UI | at least two, compared blind | per-criterion, then adjudication, then options analysis | . | As-is: an existing visualiser, drawn as it renders on main | exactly one, marked as-is | the same criteria. A finding becomes a work item against the visualiser, not a redesign | .

81add79c9dbe.title: 1. Intent
81add79c9dbe.content: A few sentences: who the screen is for, what they need to do, and what it must show. For an as-is wireframe, the intent is read off the visualiser’s own declaration and generator, not invented.

f3afb03cd68a.title: 2. Candidates
f3afb03cd68a.content: . | Mid-fidelity HTML: monochrome, real content from the graph it shows, semantic icons, and no placeholder text. | Web and mobile in every candidate, through responsive CSS or two layouts. A candidate with one layout does not enter review. | .

ca6e65b47b4a.title: 3. Mechanical checks (wireframe-viewport-check)
ca6e65b47b4a.content: bun run cat wireframe:check --use as-is --topic <topic> --surface <visualiser ref> bun run cat wireframe:check --use design --topic <slug> --surface <surface> . The three flags are this skill’s input. --topic picks the directory in the table above and every candidate in it (name candidates to check fewer; one outside it is refused), and the report goes to its checks/. --use design needs at least two candidates; --use as-is needs each marked as-is in its file name, and a --surface that is the topic or a ref index.json says it covers. The use, topic and surface are recorded in report.json. This renders each candidate at web (1280×800) and mobile (390×844) sizes. It records script entries for renders, no-overflow and no-placeholder, each pass or fail with a note, and writes a screenshot per viewport. Any fail sends the candidate back to step 2.

73f28e59c9ff.title: 4. Blind review, per criterion
73f28e59c9ff.content: Reviewers include at least one agent that did not author the candidate and one human. For Design use called from CRDM, the human is the requester or the BA who owns the request: the person who will accept the delivered feature chooses its design. They see the intent, the screenshots and the HTML, without the authors. For each criterion they record pass, warn or fail, with a reason: . | criterion | question | . | intent-fit | Does it do what the intent says, for the person it names? | . | web usability | Can the task be done at desktop width? | . | mobile usability | Can the task be done at phone width, by touch? | . | accessibility | Contrast, a non-colour channel, accessible names, keyboard, reading order | . | alternatives | Do the candidates differ in the ways that matter? (Design use only) | . There are no scores and no averages (methodology-adoption, Refusals).

91c019c3d9b6.title: 5. Adjudication and choice
91c019c3d9b6.content: . | When entries for one criterion disagree, call Process_Adjudication. The adjudication leads, the checker’s entry is kept, and a dispensation needs its reason. | The choice between surviving candidates is Process_OptionsAnalysis. Rejected candidates stay, each with the reason it lost. | .

401ba143cd39.title: Staging links
401ba143cd39.content: When a staging preview exists, every request this skill makes for feedback, review or sign-off carries it: one deep link per changed page, to the anchor where the change sits, with the same page on main as before. Where the skill declares an output contract, they go in its stagingLinks field. The rule, and where the page list comes from: feedback-deep-links.

94e5f49d9197.title: Showing it to the requester
94e5f49d9197.content: Design use from CRDM ends in a person’s choice, so the candidates must be in front of that person before implementation starts: . | Commit the candidates, intent.md, checks/ (screenshots) and reviews/ under docs/proposals/<slug>/wireframes/ on the feature branch, so feature-staging publishes them with the rest of the branch. | Show them where the requester will look, chosen from context: the conversation, the issue the request came from, the pull request, or more than one of these. Where it goes is a judgement (feedback-deep-links, point 5); every place chosen carries the same content: a short narrative of what each candidate does differently; branches/ deep links to each candidate’s HTML (not the site root); and its web and mobile screenshots shown as images, not only linked. Say which could not be linked or rendered, and why. | Ask the requester or BA to choose, with the comparison (one row per candidate, from A_CompareOptions) and a recommendation, per interaction-modality where it applies. | Record their choice in the proposal and in the output’s chosen. An agent never chooses on their behalf. Implementation (CRDM Phase 6) builds against the chosen candidate, and the delivery summary links it beside the after-screenshot. | .
